newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle program faces safety questions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle program faces safety questions.

text.p: The U.S. space agency's efforts to cut the cost of the shuttle program could lead to increased safety risks, an independent report said on Friday.

The Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel said shuttle flight safety could be jeopardized as NASA scales back its safety inspections and hands over more responsibility for the running of the shuttle program to a single private contractor.

Since the 1986 Challenger accident NASA employees have worked side-by-side with contractors so possible safety issues could be identified immediately. Under the new single contractor this arrangement will be replaced by spot checks and audits by NASA officials.

"Periodic independent assessment activities, audits and analyses of metrics are not sufficient to provide the degree of independent oversight required to operate the space shuttle program at minimum risk levels," the report said.
The safety panel said contractors would be less likely to report potential safety problems and urged NASA to retain its presence on the work floor.

The 18-day flight of space shuttle Columbia which ended on December 7 was the first to be conducted under the single contractor, United Space Alliance of Houston, a joint venture of Lockheed Martin Corp. and Boeing Corp.
"NASA should not be misled by the apparent initial success of all of the transition efforts," the report stated.
Although the contract with United Space Alliance came into effect on October 1, the planned changes to the space agency's independent safety program have yet to be made, the panel said.
NASA Administrator Daniel Goldin said in a statement the report had given the space shuttle program a clean bill of health.

"The panel also pointed out some areas for continuing emphasis and the need to improve," he added. "NASA concurs with these findings and I have instructed the institutional management and the space shuttle program to implement them as soon as possible."
The Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel report was commissioned by NASA at the request of the White House.
